entries.title: Associations of Physical Activity and Diet Quality With Mortality and Cardiovascular Disease in Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome
entries.abstract: BACKGROUND: Physical activity (PA) and diet are cornerstones for cardiovascular disease (CVD) prevention, yet their associations with CVD within the cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) framework remain unexplored. OBJECTIVES: This study aims to evaluate the independent and joint associations of PA and/or diet quality with mortality and incident CVD across CKM stages. METHODS: Our study included 339,074 UK Biobank participants (51.3% women, mean age 56.4 years) with CKM syndrome stage 0 to 4. PA was categorized as high (≥150 min/wk of walking or moderate-to-vigorous activity) or low using self-reported and accelerometer-measured data. Diet quality was classified as low/median/high. Cox proportional hazards models assessed associations with incident CVD, cause-specific CVD mortality, and all-cause mortality across CKM stages. RESULTS: High PA was associated with lower risks of all-cause mortality (HR: 0.76 [95% CI: 0.74-0.79]), composite CVD mortality (0.74 [0.70-0.77]), and incident composite CVD (0.90 [0.88-0.92]); for high diet quality, corresponding HRs (95% CIs) were 0.81 (0.77-0.85), 0.81 (0.75-0.88), and 0.87 (0.84-0.90). PA showed nonlinear associations with these outcomes, plateauing at approximately 2,500 metabolic equivalent min/wk. High PA combined with high diet quality showed stronger inverse associations with all-cause mortality (0.64 [0.60-0.68]), composite CVD mortality (0.61 [0.54-0.68]), and incident composite CVD (0.83 [0.79-0.88]). Significant multiplicative interactions between PA and diet quality were observed for stroke mortality, composite CVD, and heart failure. The joint associations with these outcomes were stronger at more advanced CKM syndrome stages. CONCLUSIONS: Beyond individual benefits, joint PA-diet modification was associated with lower risk of mortality and CVD across CKM stages, highlighting the value of integrated behavioral strategies.

entries.title: An Opinion Paper on the Cultural Heritage of Wine Consumption in the Frame of the Mediterranean Diet: The Missing Piece of the Puzzle
entries.abstract: The role of wine within the Mediterranean diet remains one of the most debated and paradoxical issues in nutritional epidemiology. Although moderate wine consumption, particularly alongside meals, has traditionally been incorporated into Mediterranean diet scores and has been associated with lower cardiovascular and all-cause mortality, alcohol is also an established carcinogen, with evidence of increased cancer risk even at relatively low levels of consumption. This apparent contradiction has renewed the debate over whether wine represents a genuine protective component of the Mediterranean diet or whether its observed associations reflect methodological and contextual factors. In this opinion paper, we critically examine emerging evidence on wine consumption, the Mediterranean dietary pattern and the Mediterranean alcohol-drinking pattern, with particular attention to the limitations of observational alcohol epidemiology, including abstainer-reference bias, reverse causation, exposure misclassification and the divergence between observational and Mendelian randomization evidence. Additionally, drawing on the concept of the traditional Mediterranean lifestyle, we further propose that moderation and synergy between lifestyle components may be more informative than the isolated attribution of health effects to individual foods or beverages. Thus, instead of searching for a “hidden virtue” in wine itself, the more relevant hypothesis may be that of a “hidden context”, whereby the health associations attributed to moderate wine consumption are inseparable from the broader Mediterranean lifestyle in which it is embedded.
